paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation gives a language model access to documents, but attaching a citation does not ensure that the cited material supports a statement. CiteGuard addresses this gap with a decoding layer that decides which sentence-level claims have enough evidence to include and which should be withheld.

The method frames these decisions as a collection of statistical tests. It converts claim–evidence scores into calibrated p-values under the hypothesis that a claim is unsupported. It then applies BH/BY procedures to control false discoveries among accepted claims. This connects individual evidence assessments to an overall risk budget, rather than treating every citation as independently trustworthy.

On FEVER and Natural Questions, CiteGuard lowers the reported false-discovery rate from 28–31% for vanilla RAG to below 10% at a risk setting of 0.10, while retaining 86–92% of supported claims. Users can adjust that setting to trade coverage against faithfulness. The finite-sample guarantees depend on standard exchangeability assumptions; they do not promise that every accepted claim is supported.
icml-2026-citeguard-conformal-false-disc.tldr: CiteGuard statistically filters RAG claims to control the rate of unsupported statements while retaining most supported claims in its evaluations.

paragraphs: CoD-Lite studies how to build a diffusion image codec small and fast enough for real-time compression. The paper questions whether design choices that work for large image generators also work under these tighter constraints. It focuses on two choices: what the model should learn during pretraining, and whether its architecture needs transformers.

The analysis finds that generation-oriented pretraining is less effective at small model scales, whereas compression-oriented pretraining performs consistently better. It also finds that lightweight convolutions can suffice for compression-oriented diffusion when combined with distillation. These findings motivate a convolutional codec that performs its diffusion computation in one step, with further improvements from distillation and adversarial learning.

The resulting codec achieves reported speeds of 60 frames per second for encoding and 42 for decoding at 1080p. It also uses 85% less bitrate than MS-ILLM at comparable FID. That comparison concerns the stated FID measure, rather than establishing equivalence on every aspect of reconstruction quality. The contribution is a compression-specific design supported by both analysis and real-time performance results.
icml-2026-cod-lite-real-time-diffusion-b.tldr: CoD-Lite combines compression-oriented pretraining, convolutions, and distillation to deliver a lightweight one-step diffusion codec with real-time 1080p performance.

paragraphs: AI debate aims to help a judge evaluate competing answers, but it can reward persuasive arguments even when they are not epistemically honest. This paper explores a different interaction protocol for scalable oversight: have models work together to understand and resolve their disagreements.

The proposed automated pipeline draws on mediation and conflict resolution. Models identify the claims on which they differ, inspect the evidence behind those claims, and try to reach agreement. When agreement remains out of reach, they isolate the specific crux keeping their positions apart. This changes the task from defending a fixed position to clarifying what the disagreement actually depends on.

In the reported experiments, disagreement resolution helps non-expert models judge truth more accurately, reaching 62.1% judging accuracy compared with 49.2% for standard debate. The findings support collaborative examination as a promising oversight protocol. They provide empirical evidence that changing how models interact can improve judgments, without establishing that consensus itself is a guarantee of truth.
icml-2026-collaborative-disagreement-res.tldr: A collaborative disagreement-resolution protocol improves non-expert models’ judging accuracy over standard adversarial debate in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: DriveWorld-VLA connects autonomous-driving planning with a model of how the surrounding scene may evolve. The paper identifies insufficient sharing of internal representations as a weakness in existing combinations of vision–language–action systems and world models. If imagined futures are poorly connected to planning, they have limited influence on action decisions.

The framework makes the world model’s latent states central to the planner’s decisions. These states are internal feature representations of the scene, allowing the planner to assess how candidate actions affect future developments. World modeling takes place entirely in this latent space, supporting action-conditioned imagination without generating expensive sequences of future pixels. The shared representation also reduces reliance on dense annotated supervision.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance across open-loop and closed-loop evaluations: 91.3 PDMS on NAVSIMv1, 86.8 EPDMS on NAVSIMv2, and a 0.16 three-second average collision rate on nuScenes. These findings support the value of tightly connecting scene prediction and planning at the representation level, so future modeling directly informs the decision process.
icml-2026-driveworld-vla-unified-latent-.tldr: DriveWorld-VLA shares latent states between world modeling and action planning to make imagined scene evolution directly useful for autonomous-driving decisions.

paragraphs: SyNGLER generates synthetic networks while aiming to preserve structural properties of an observed network. The motivation is that some black-box generators overfit the available data, miss characteristic network structure, and become computationally expensive at scale. The proposed framework organizes generation around a low-dimensional representation of the network’s nodes.

First, a latent space network model learns an embedding for each node. SyNGLER then builds a distribution-free generator over those embeddings to reconstruct the latent space. To produce a new network, it samples or resamples node embeddings and uses the latent space model to generate connections. This separates learning a useful representation from producing new configurations of nodes and edges.

The framework preserves properties such as sparsity and variation in node degrees while requiring less training computation than many existing deep architectures. The paper develops consistency results concerning the distance between true and synthetic edge distributions. Empirical studies also show better preservation of network moments and degree distributions than existing approaches, supporting both the efficiency and structural usefulness of the design.
icml-2026-efficient-synthetic-network-ge.tldr: SyNGLER generates networks through sampled latent node embeddings, preserving key structural properties with relatively low computational cost.

paragraphs: EmBrace addresses the problem of combining EEG foundation models whose strengths differ across tasks and individual samples. The authors observe that no single model consistently performs best on every task. They also find that a model with weaker overall task performance can still be useful on particular samples because different architectures develop different inductive biases.

The framework combines intermediate representations rather than requiring models to align their parameters or final outputs. It brings discriminative internal representations into a shared space and adaptively weights the participating models for each sample. It also selects the most compatible model as the carrier for the fused knowledge. This makes the combination responsive to sample-level differences rather than relying solely on an overall ranking.

Experiments across multiple EEG benchmarks show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art EEG foundation models and effective generalization across tasks. The results support the paper’s central observation: useful knowledge can remain in models that are not the strongest overall. Representation-level fusion offers a way to capture those complementary strengths.
icml-2026-embrace-a-collective-knowledge.tldr: EmBrace combines EEG models’ intermediate representations with sample-specific weights to exploit strengths that overall model rankings can miss.

paragraphs: Diagnostic-driven Progressive Evolution, or DPE, makes multimodal model training responsive to the model’s current weaknesses. The paper argues that static datasets and fixed training recipes make it difficult to identify capability blind spots and direct reinforcement toward them. Its alternative is a repeating cycle of diagnosis, targeted training, and renewed diagnosis.

Multiple agents annotate and check the quality of large amounts of unlabeled multimodal data. They use tools including web search and image editing to produce diverse, realistic samples. A second component attributes model failures to specific weaknesses, adjusts the training-data mixture, and directs the agents to generate examples focused on those weaknesses. Each updated model is examined again to determine the next round of training.

Experiments with Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct show stable, continuing gains across eleven benchmarks. These results support diagnosis as a practical signal for steering data generation and reinforcement over successive iterations. The claimed benefit comes from repeatedly adapting training to observed failures as the model changes.
icml-2026-from-blind-spots-to-gains-diag.tldr: DPE repeatedly diagnoses multimodal model weaknesses and generates targeted training data, producing continued gains across eleven evaluated benchmarks.

paragraphs: HiMe targets robotic tasks where the current observation alone does not contain enough information to choose the next action. Such tasks require remembering earlier events and maintaining a longer-term strategy. The paper also addresses a timing conflict: capable reasoning models can be too slow for real-time control, while faster models may reason less effectively.

The framework separates responsibilities among three components. A high-frequency Executor handles execution, a Sentry maintains working memory, and a Planner manages long-term strategy. A dynamic knowledge system organizes information through cross-modal semantic schemas and actively adds, updates, or deletes stored knowledge. Memory can therefore change as the robot’s situation and understanding develop.

This hierarchy gives fast control and slower planning distinct roles while connecting them through memory. The experiments report significantly better success rates on long-horizon tasks and improvements over flat memory baselines. They also demonstrate an ability to correct internal knowledge based on human preferences, showing that the stored information can be revised through interaction.
icml-2026-hime-hierarchical-embodied-mem.tldr: HiMe separates fast execution, working memory, and long-term planning to improve robotic control on tasks requiring persistent, revisable knowledge.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts models can increase total parameter capacity without activating every parameter for each token. However, they introduce additional tuning decisions, including router weights, the number of experts, and expert size. This paper aims to make hyperparameter selection cheaper by allowing settings found on small models to transfer reliably to larger ones.

The authors propose a parameterization for transformers with mixture-of-experts layers that accounts for changes in width, depth, expert count, and expert hidden size. A new dynamical mean-field theory analysis provides the justification. The central idea is to organize model scaling so hyperparameters remain useful as several architectural dimensions change, reducing the need to search independently at every scale.

With a fixed training-token budget, experiments show reliable hyperparameter transfer across models ranging from 51 million to 2 billion total parameters. The authors also use settings selected through short training sweeps on small models to train larger models for longer, reporting performant behavior. The evidence therefore covers both architectural scaling and an additional transfer to longer training horizons.
icml-2026-hyperparameter-transfer-with-m.tldr: A theoretically justified MoE parameterization enables empirically reliable hyperparameter transfer across multiple architectural dimensions and model sizes.

paragraphs: REPA-P addresses a weakness in physics-informed diffusion models: applying physical constraints only to final outputs leaves intermediate representations unconstrained. The paper connects this gap to shortcut learning when boundary conditions change. Its approach teaches selected internal layers to represent physical states during training.

Lightweight 1×1 projection heads convert hidden activations into physical quantities. The training objective then applies partial differential equation residual losses to those quantities, measuring their agreement with the governing equations. The method requires no teacher model and can be attached to different architectures. The heads are removed for inference, so this extra supervision adds no inference overhead.

Across Darcy flow, topology optimization, electrostatic potential, and turbulent channel flow, REPA-P reports up to twice-faster convergence, up to 66.4% lower physics residuals, and up to 49.3% better out-of-distribution robustness. Gains appear on both U-Net and Diffusion Transformer backbones. Ablations indicate that supervising only a small selection of intermediate layers captures most benefits and complements physical constraints on final outputs.
icml-2026-learning-to-think-in-physics-b.tldr: REPA-P supervises diffusion models’ intermediate features with physical equations, improving reported robustness and convergence without adding inference cost.

paragraphs: Classifier-free guidance steers conditional diffusion generation, but strong guidance can cause oversaturated outputs, texture artifacts, and structural collapse. This paper attributes those failures to geometry: ordinary guidance extrapolates in the surrounding space and can push sampling trajectories away from the high-density region associated with the data.

Manifold-Optimal Guidance, or MOG, reformulates guidance as a local optimal-control problem. It derives a closed-form Riemannian update that accounts for the geometry of that data region and corrects drift away from it. The update requires no retraining, making the contribution a change to how generation is guided rather than an additional model-training procedure.

The authors also introduce Auto-MOG, which adjusts guidance strength through a dynamic energy-balancing schedule. They report that it effectively removes the need to tune guidance strength manually. Extensive validation finds better fidelity and alignment than the evaluated baselines with virtually no additional computation. Together, the results support geometry-aware updates and adaptive strength selection as useful ways to improve conditional diffusion guidance.
icml-2026-manifold-optimal-guidance-a-un.tldr: MOG uses geometry-aware diffusion guidance to reduce off-manifold drift, while Auto-MOG adaptively selects guidance strength.

paragraphs: MAST tackles the reconstruction of molecular structures from spectra, where ambiguous measurements and a vast space of possible molecules make inference difficult. The paper identifies two problems with existing diffusion approaches: global spectral representations can be difficult to learn from limited paired data, and repeatedly performing full sampling runs is computationally costly.

The framework introduces explicit molecular motif priors as interpretable intermediate evidence throughout denoising. These structural clues reduce ambiguity and help guide optimization toward molecules consistent with the spectra. MAST also turns sampling into reward-guided tree search, prioritizing promising denoising trajectories to produce a compact set of candidates within a limited computational budget.

MAST jointly addresses two-dimensional molecular structure and three-dimensional geometry. On the QM9S multi-spectra benchmark, it achieves 94.89% exact recovery and improves 3D fidelity while preserving high chemical validity and stability. The findings support combining intermediate structural evidence with selective search: the model receives more informative guidance, and inference concentrates computation on promising candidate-generation paths.
icml-2026-mast-motif-augmented-diffusion.tldr: MAST combines interpretable motif guidance with reward-guided diffusion search to recover molecular structures from spectra efficiently.

paragraphs: MetaMoE combines independently trained, domain-specialized experts when their original training data cannot be shared. Conventional mixture-of-experts training often assumes centralized access to data, creating a difficulty when expertise is distributed across clients with privacy constraints. The framework uses public proxy data to stand in for the inaccessible private datasets.

Its central mechanism selects public samples for both relevance to client domains and diversity. These proxies approximate the private data distributions and provide supervision for learning the router that chooses experts. They also help align expert training so the specialists coordinate more effectively when unified. A context-aware router further adapts expert selection to heterogeneous inputs.

Experiments on computer vision and natural language processing benchmarks show consistent improvements over recent privacy-preserving MoE unification methods. The findings support proxy selection as an important part of joining separately trained models: public examples must represent different domains while also covering diverse cases. The framework’s stated privacy setting keeps original client training data inaccessible during this unification process.
icml-2026-metamoe-diversity-aware-proxy-.tldr: MetaMoE uses relevant, diverse public proxy data to coordinate private-domain experts and train a unified context-aware router.

paragraphs: This paper studies the statistical efficiency of multi-armed bandit learning with a KL-regularized objective. Regret measures accumulated shortfall relative to the objective’s benchmark. Prior work suggests regularization can produce faster learning rates, but the dependence on the number of choices, training duration, and regularization strength was not fully characterized.

Using a new peeling argument, the authors sharpen the analysis of KL-UCB. They establish a high-probability regret upper bound of approximately ηK log² T, hiding other logarithmic factors, where K is the number of arms, T the horizon, and 1/η the regularization intensity. This is the first such bound with linear dependence on K. A lower bound of order ηK log T shows the analysis is nearly tight.

The behavior changes when regularization is weak, meaning η is large. In that regime, regret becomes independent of η and scales approximately as the square root of KT. The combined results explain both the benefits of stronger regularization and the transition to familiar bandit scaling under weak regularization.
icml-2026-near-optimal-regret-for-kl-reg.tldr: The paper establishes nearly matching regret bounds for KL-regularized bandits and characterizes their transition to square-root scaling under weak regularization.

paragraphs: Multi-objective combinatorial optimization involves finding discrete solutions while accounting for several objectives. Decomposition-based methods address subproblems associated with particular preferences over those objectives. This paper argues that existing methods leave useful structure underrepresented because they focus on nodes and overlook the complementary information carried by edges.

The proposed attention mechanism combines node and edge features in a preference-sensitive way. It first uses preference-modulated edge features as explicit biases in attention, helping the model recognize structure relevant to the current subproblem. It also updates edge representations with node-specific context through a dynamic aggregation strategy. Information therefore flows between representations of individual nodes and their relationships.

Experiments on classic multi-objective combinatorial optimization benchmarks report better performance and generalization than the compared approaches. The findings support making structural relationships depend explicitly on objective preferences. Rather than representing a problem instance identically for every trade-off, the mechanism lets the requested balance among objectives influence which relationships receive attention.
icml-2026-preference-modulated-structura.tldr: Preference-modulated attention combines node and edge information to improve representations and reported results for multi-objective combinatorial optimization.

paragraphs: PRISM seeks to combine expressive sequence modeling with efficient parallel computation. The paper identifies limitations in shallow linear updates and a different bottleneck in iterative methods such as Test-Time Training: dependencies across both tokens and optimization steps restrict hardware parallelism.

The proposed architecture reconstructs the gate, residual, and direction pattern of iterative correction in a feedforward form. A Write-Forget Decoupling strategy isolates nonlinearity within the injection operator. A short convolution then anchors an initial residual using local history, while a learned predictor estimates refinement updates directly from the input. This two-stage proxy captures structural patterns of correction without executing the corresponding serial solver loops.

The theoretical analysis establishes Rank-L accumulation, expanding the update structure beyond a single-step Rank-1 bottleneck. Empirically, PRISM achieves performance comparable to explicit optimization methods while delivering 174 times higher throughput in the reported comparison. The contribution links a more expressive update structure with an architecture designed to preserve parallel execution.
icml-2026-prism-parallel-residual-iterat.tldr: PRISM approximates iterative sequence-model corrections with a parallel feedforward architecture, reporting comparable performance and 174-fold higher throughput.

paragraphs: Unsupervised pretext tasks help models learn from unlabeled data, but their usefulness depends on whether their underlying assumptions fit the model, data, and eventual target task. This paper asks whether that fit can be evaluated cheaply before committing to extensive training and validation.

The theoretical analysis identifies three factors governing the effect on target performance. Learnability concerns whether the model can learn the assumption embedded in the pretext task. Reliability concerns whether that assumption holds for the data. Completeness concerns whether it adequately serves the target task. This decomposition turns a broad question about pretext-task suitability into three distinct aspects of compatibility.

Building on the derivation, the authors propose a low-cost method for quantitatively estimating target performance. They evaluate it using a benchmark containing more than one hundred pretext tasks. The estimates strongly correlate with performance obtained through large-scale training and validation. That finding supports the method as a way to assess likely usefulness in advance, while the reported result is correlation rather than perfect prediction.
icml-2026-quantitative-estimation-of-tar.tldr: The paper estimates pretext-task usefulness through assumption learnability, reliability, and completeness, with predictions strongly correlating with measured target performance.

paragraphs: SALE accelerates the prefilling stage in which a language model processes a long input. Full self-attention becomes expensive because its computation grows quadratically with sequence length. Sparse methods skip less important attention regions, but the paper argues that coarse inspection can miss the detail needed for a good accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

SALE estimates attention at finer granularity using low-bit quantized query-key products. A Relative Attention Score then assesses the importance of query-key pairs and determines a highly sparse attention mask. The purpose of the cheap estimate is to identify where the more costly attention computation matters. A custom CUDA kernel keeps the method’s overhead to approximately 11% of full-attention latency.

The method requires no parameter training and is designed for integration with small code changes. Long-context experiments report better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs than existing approaches. On Llama-3.1-8B, sequences longer than 64K achieve at least 3.36-fold speedups while maintaining model quality. These results support inexpensive, fine-grained inspection as a practical basis for sparse attention.
icml-2026-sale-low-bit-estimation-for-ef.tldr: SALE uses low-bit attention estimates to select important computations, speeding long-context prefilling with negligible reported accuracy loss.

paragraphs: SC-FAGC addresses scalable clustering with explicit control over cluster sizes. Standard spectral clustering has cubic time complexity in the number of data points. Anchor-based approximations reduce the computational burden by using far fewer representative anchors, but can produce trivial or highly unbalanced partitions when sizes are not controlled.

The method combines entropy regularization with user-specified lower and upper bounds on anchor-level cluster sizes. To optimize the resulting non-convex objective, it uses an iteratively reweighted procedure that linearizes the objective. Each subproblem is handled by a double-bounded optimal-transport solver based on the Sinkhorn–Knopp algorithm. The authors establish convergence for the optimization scheme while maintaining scalability.

Benchmark experiments report state-of-the-art results across six clustering metrics and strict satisfaction of the prescribed anchor-level size constraints. Transferring labels from anchors to data points also produces effective data-level size control. The distinction matters: the explicit constraints apply to anchor groups, while the reported control over full-data group sizes arises after label transmission.
icml-2026-sc-fagc-size-constrained-fast-.tldr: SC-FAGC adds explicit anchor-level size bounds to scalable spectral clustering, improving reported clustering quality while controlling partition balance.

paragraphs: This paper explores whether better reasoning can be obtained by changing how a language model samples answers, without further training. Its motivation is evidence suggesting that much of reinforcement-learning post-training’s benefit comes from sharpening an existing output distribution. Earlier power-distribution sampling approaches recover comparable performance, but their iterative MCMC procedures are expensive.

The authors derive an approximation to the global power distribution using token-level, scaled low-temperature sampling. The scaling factor captures the quality of future trajectories, connecting each local token choice to the quality of possible continuations. This produces an autoregressive algorithm that sharpens the base model’s distribution without requiring training, a verifier, or external rewards.

Evaluations on mathematics, question answering, and code show that the method matches or exceeds one-shot GRPO while reducing inference latency by more than tenfold relative to MCMC-based sampling. The results support a cheaper sampling route to reasoning improvements in those evaluations. The theoretical contribution explains how a sequence-level sampling objective can be approximated through token-level decisions.
icml-2026-scalable-power-sampling-unlock.tldr: A training-free token-level approximation to power sampling matches or exceeds one-shot GRPO in evaluations with over tenfold lower latency than MCMC sampling.

paragraphs: Sparse ActionGen accelerates diffusion policies used to generate robotic actions. These policies can represent multiple possible action patterns, but repeated denoising steps make real-time control difficult. Existing methods reuse cached computations on static schedules, which may not adapt well as the robot and its environment interact.

The proposed prune-then-reuse mechanism first identifies computations that can be removed across the action-generation process, then substitutes cached activations during diffusion. An observation-conditioned pruner adapts these decisions to the current environment and rollout. Its design is efficient in both parameters and inference, keeping the adaptation itself suitable for real-time prediction.

A further reuse strategy shares activations across both denoising timesteps and network blocks in a zig-zag pattern to reduce overall redundancy. Across multiple robotic benchmarks, Sparse ActionGen reports action-generation speedups of up to fourfold without sacrificing performance. The findings support adapting computation reuse to the ongoing interaction, so acceleration decisions can reflect changing observations rather than depending only on a fixed schedule.
icml-2026-sparse-actiongen-accelerating-.tldr: Sparse ActionGen adapts pruning and activation reuse to robot observations, achieving up to fourfold faster action generation without reported performance loss.

paragraphs: CT-LLM models text generation using an internal state that evolves continuously in time. The generated text still consists of discrete tokens, but the framework represents the semantic evolution underlying those choices through continuous latent dynamics. The paper’s central contribution is a formulation connecting these two kinds of representation.

Token generation is expressed as a Markov decision process, with the internal state governed by a neural ordinary differential equation. Reinforcement learning optimizes the framework using an objective that combines cumulative rewards with KL-divergence regularization relative to a pretrained language model. The objective therefore brings together reward-driven generation and a term that constrains divergence from an existing language model.

The authors report both theoretical and empirical results supporting improved effectiveness and efficiency in text generation. Those findings support continuous-time latent states as a viable basis for language modeling within their framework. The proposed approach changes how the internal generation process is represented and optimized, while maintaining the connection to discrete token decisions and pretrained-model regularization.
icml-2026-text-generation-as-continuous-.tldr: CT-LLM combines neural-ODE latent dynamics with reinforcement learning to connect continuous internal evolution and discrete text generation.

paragraphs: VT-Bench focuses on learning from images together with tabular data, an area the paper describes as underexplored compared with image-and-text learning. This combination matters in domains such as healthcare and industry. The contribution is a unified benchmark intended to standardize evaluation across both discriminative prediction and generative reasoning tasks.

The benchmark brings together 14 datasets from nine domains, totaling more than 756,000 samples. Its emphasis is medical, while its coverage also includes pets, media, and transportation. Bringing these datasets into a common benchmark creates a shared basis for examining how models handle visual and structured information across different task settings.

The authors evaluate 23 representative models, including unimodal experts, specialized visual-tabular systems, general-purpose vision-language models, and methods augmented with tools. The evaluation highlights substantial remaining challenges in visual-tabular learning. The benchmark’s role is to make those challenges more consistently measurable and support future development of models that can work effectively with this combination of modalities.
icml-2026-vt-bench-a-unified-benchmark-f.tldr: VT-Bench standardizes visual-tabular prediction and reasoning evaluation across 14 datasets and assesses 23 representative models.

paragraphs: This paper studies why diffusion models can help recover signals even when their training data differ from the target or their generative quality is limited. Such models serve as weak priors in inverse problems. The authors investigate the surprising observation that these priors can sometimes perform nearly as well as stronger models trained on matching data.

Experiments find that weak priors succeed when measurements are highly informative, such as when many pixels are observed, and also identify regimes where they fail. The explanation combines Bayesian-consistency theory with analysis of local spatial correlations. The theory gives conditions under which high-dimensional measurements concentrate the posterior near the true signal, while the correlation analysis shows that weak and strong natural-image priors can share useful local structure.

The contribution is a conditional account of robustness to prior mismatch. Informative measurements and shared spatial structure can make a weak diffusion prior useful despite its shortcomings. This supports using such priors in suitable regimes while preserving the paper’s finding that their reliability does not extend to every inverse problem.
icml-2026-weak-diffusion-priors-can-stil.tldr: Weak diffusion priors can support strong signal recovery when measurements are informative, with theory and local-correlation analysis explaining this conditional robustness.

paragraphs: VeMo evaluates whether a generated human motion matches its text description. The paper argues that existing metrics often miss this semantic correspondence. Its approach renders motion into video and uses pretrained video-language models to judge alignment, avoiding the need to train an evaluator on scarce motion-specific labels.

The framework uses normalized likelihood-based scoring to transfer the video-language models’ semantic capabilities to motion evaluation. Because projecting three-dimensional motion into a two-dimensional video can make an action ambiguous, VeMo adds entropy-driven uncertainty analysis to identify reliable views. The rendering viewpoint thus becomes part of the evaluation method rather than an incidental presentation choice.

The authors also introduce a test-only, human-annotated benchmark for evaluating the evaluators, using motions from multiple representative generation models. Experiments show stronger correlation with human judgments than existing reference-based and reference-free metrics. Analyses of view selection, rendering, prompt robustness, and computational trade-offs further characterize the approach. The stated benefit is better agreement with human assessment, with rendering and viewing choices explicitly examined.
icml-2026-zero-shot-text-to-motion-evalu.tldr: VeMo evaluates text-motion alignment through rendered videos and pretrained video-language models, correlating better with human judgments than existing metrics.
